title: The Xbox Reset Explained: What Happens to Halo, Forza, Fallout, Rare and Ninja Theory Now?
description: Microsoft’s latest Xbox restructuring moves major studios under Activision and Bethesda, combines Playground with Turn 10, cuts 268 roles, and puts Ninja Theory at risk of closure. Here is what actually changed and what each move means.
body:
Xbox’s latest restructuring is not a normal round of studio reporting-line changes. It redraws how some of Microsoft’s most recognizable game franchises are organized.

In a company-wide memo published on [Xbox Wire on September 22](https://news.xbox.com/en-us/2026/09/22/continuing-our-reset/), Microsoft confirmed **268 role eliminations** across Halo Studios, other first-party teams and Xbox Game Studios management. It also announced a new operating structure that puts Rare and World’s Edge under Activision, expands Bethesda’s remit to Obsidian, combines Playground Games and Turn 10, and begins consultation over a proposed closure of Ninja Theory after two sale agreements fell through.

The company describes the changes as part of the larger Xbox reset announced in July, when it said approximately **3,200 roles would be reduced throughout FY27** and several studios would leave Microsoft ownership. In that [July reset memo](https://news.xbox.com/en-us/2026/07/06/resetting-xbox/), Xbox argued that its studio organization had become too fragmented, management layers had grown too deep and the business needed fewer units with clearer accountability.

September’s announcement is where that theory becomes concrete.

Instead of treating every first-party studio as a largely separate organization, Xbox is clustering teams under larger publishing groups that already know how to run particular kinds of businesses. That creates obvious efficiencies. It also concentrates an enormous amount of creative responsibility inside Activision, Bethesda and a smaller number of leadership structures.

Here is what actually changed — and what each move could mean.
author: Rouane Mounssif
imageAlt: Xbox branding and first-party game imagery representing Microsoft’s studio portfolio.

contentBlocks.heading: Halo moves under Activision — but not into Call of Duty
contentBlocks.text:
The headline change is Halo.

Microsoft says Activision will develop the next Halo title through **a new purpose-built team separate from ongoing Call of Duty development**. A smaller team at Halo Studios will remain responsible for supporting current games and the existing community.

That is a structural reset of responsibility. Halo Studios is no longer being asked to carry the entire future of the franchise while also maintaining what is already live. Activision becomes accountable for the next mainline release.

The immediate fear is that Halo becomes more like Call of Duty. There is no evidence of that yet. The more grounded implication is that Halo now sits inside an organization with enormous production, QA, publishing and live-operations capacity.

I explore that distinction in more detail in [our Halo analysis](story:halo-activision-future-what-it-means): the opportunity is not annualization. It is giving Halo a development structure capable of shipping a complete game and supporting it consistently.

Whether that production discipline strengthens Halo or homogenizes it will depend on the authority of the new team.

contentBlocks.caption: Halo’s next mainline game will be built by a new Activision-led team, while a smaller Halo Studios group supports current games. Credit: Xbox / Halo Studios.

contentBlocks.heading: Rare and World’s Edge also move under Activision
contentBlocks.text:
Halo is not Activision’s only new responsibility. Microsoft says Activision will also expand its remit to **Rare** and **World’s Edge**.

That is a striking combination because the studios represent very different types of work. Rare has Sea of Thieves and one of the most recognizable histories in Microsoft’s portfolio. World’s Edge operates around Age of Empires and strategy publishing. Activision now becomes a larger umbrella for teams that have almost nothing to do with Call of Duty creatively.

This reinforces the idea that Microsoft is using Activision primarily as a **publishing and operating structure**, not as a genre template.

The potential upside is clearer shared production support and fewer isolated management layers. The risk is that studios with unusual creative cultures begin answering to an organization whose incentives were built around enormous recurring franchises.

Rare in particular will be worth watching. Sea of Thieves succeeded partly because the studio was allowed to grow a strange, social game over years rather than forcing it into a familiar first-party mold. A successful reorganization should preserve that independence while improving the machinery around it.

contentBlocks.heading: Bethesda gets Obsidian — and Fallout becomes the obvious connective tissue
contentBlocks.text:
Bethesda’s remit now expands to include **Obsidian Entertainment**. Microsoft says Obsidian will continue its current projects, including Grounded, while also working on a new Fallout project in collaboration with Bethesda Game Studios.

This is one of the easier moves to understand strategically. Bethesda already owns Fallout, while Obsidian’s Fallout: New Vegas remains one of the most discussed entries in the series. Putting the studios inside the same organizational umbrella reduces the number of corporate boundaries around future collaboration.

But the move should not be reduced to “Obsidian becomes a Fallout studio.” Obsidian has spent years building its own identity across The Outer Worlds, Grounded, Avowed and smaller experimental projects. The value of bringing it closer to Bethesda is the possibility of sharing technology, production infrastructure and franchise expertise without flattening that portfolio.

The new Fallout collaboration will be the first obvious test. If the organizational change makes cross-studio work easier while Obsidian keeps its own creative range, the logic is strong. If every studio simply gets pulled toward the largest IP under its new parent group, Xbox becomes more efficient but less interesting.

contentBlocks.heading: Playground and Turn 10 become one studio for Forza and Fable
contentBlocks.text:
Microsoft is also formally combining **Playground Games and Turn 10** into a single studio focused on the Forza and Fable franchises.

The relationship already existed in practice. Turn 10 created Forza Motorsport and has long overseen the broader Forza technology and franchise framework, while Playground turned Forza Horizon into one of Xbox’s most successful series. Playground is also developing Fable.

The restructuring makes that partnership organizational instead of informal.

There is a practical logic here: shared engine knowledge, racing expertise, tools and production support can sit inside one structure instead of moving between two companies with separate management. But the combined studio will also carry an unusually broad mandate. Forza Motorsport, Forza Horizon and Fable have very different production needs.

The key question is whether combining leadership reduces bureaucracy or simply creates a larger studio with more competing priorities. Microsoft’s July memo argued that Xbox had accumulated too many management layers and fragmented responsibilities. This merger is a direct attempt to reverse that.

contentBlocks.heading: Ninja Theory is the most difficult part of the announcement
contentBlocks.text:
Not every change is a reorganization with an obvious future role.

Microsoft says **two separate agreements for Ninja Theory fell through**, and it will now begin consultation with employees on a proposed closure while continuing to explore other paths forward.

That language matters. A proposed closure is not the same thing as a completed closure, and consultation processes can affect the eventual outcome. But the studio’s position is clearly precarious.

This follows the July reset, when Microsoft said Ninja Theory had entered terms to join new ownership with funding intended to complete and grow Senua. Those plans did not reach completion.

The contrast with studios such as Obsidian or Rare is stark. They are being moved into new operating homes inside Xbox. Ninja Theory is still searching for one.

That uncertainty is also why it would be wrong to treat the restructuring purely as an efficiency story. Hundreds of jobs are being eliminated across the organization, and studio transitions affect people whose work cannot be reduced to a portfolio diagram.

contentBlocks.heading: The reset is concentrating Xbox around fewer operating centers
contentBlocks.text:
Taken together, the September changes make the larger strategy much easier to see.

Xbox is trying to become **less like a federation of many independently managed studios and more like a smaller number of operating groups** with explicit accountability.

Activision gets Halo, Rare and World’s Edge. Bethesda gets Obsidian. King gets Microsoft Casual Games. Playground and Turn 10 become one team. Other studios have already left Xbox ownership or entered consultation processes.

That matches the language Microsoft used in July, when it said some work was passing through as many as 14 management layers and promised to reduce that to no more than five, and where possible three. The company also said its platform teams had grown significantly while player base and playtime declined, and argued that clearer ownership was necessary.

The philosophy is straightforward: fewer reporting chains, fewer duplicated functions, fewer places where responsibility can become ambiguous.

Whether it produces better games is not straightforward at all.

contentBlocks.heading: What players should actually watch next
contentBlocks.text:
The next six to twelve months will tell us more than the organization chart.

For Halo, watch who leads the new team and what Xbox defines as a complete launch. For Rare, watch whether Sea of Thieves continues to operate with the same creative autonomy. For Obsidian, watch whether the Bethesda relationship expands collaboration without narrowing its slate. For Playground and Turn 10, watch whether the combined structure accelerates development or creates new internal competition for resources.

And for Ninja Theory, the immediate question is more fundamental: whether another path can be found before the proposed closure process reaches its conclusion.

The October 6 Xbox town hall mentioned in Microsoft’s memo may provide more internal direction, but players should resist reading every structural move as an immediate creative verdict.

Organizations can become cleaner without games becoming better. The reset will matter only if the new structure gives talented teams clearer goals, realistic schedules and enough authority to protect the identity of the games they are making.

quickRead: Xbox is eliminating 268 roles across Halo Studios, other first-party teams and Xbox Game Studios management.
Activision will oversee Rare and World’s Edge and will build the next Halo through a new purpose-built team separate from Call of Duty development.
Bethesda’s remit expands to Obsidian, including a new Fallout collaboration, while Playground and Turn 10 are being combined.
Microsoft has begun consultation over a proposed Ninja Theory closure after two sale agreements fell through.
conclusion:
Microsoft’s Xbox reset is becoming less abstract.

The July announcement described a company with too many layers, too many fragmented teams and a business model that had not grown as expected. September’s reorganization is the operational answer: concentrate studios around fewer publishing groups, move responsibility closer to organizations with proven production infrastructure and reduce the number of separate units Xbox has to manage.

That may make the company easier to run.

It does not automatically make the games better.

The strength of Xbox’s portfolio has always come from how different its studios can be. Halo should not feel like Call of Duty. Rare should not feel like Blizzard. Obsidian should not become Bethesda Game Studios with a different logo. Playground’s Fable should not be forced into the same production assumptions as Forza.

The reset succeeds only if Microsoft can simplify the organization without simplifying the creative identities inside it.
conclusionHeading: A cleaner Xbox structure only matters if the games stay distinct
